item.title: Rigorous Analysis Confirms NASA’s Artemis II Heat Shield Performance - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the Moon and brought them safely back to Earth, laying a foundation for crewed flights to the Moon’s surface.

Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected.

In particular, NASA measured whether the thermal protection system effectively safeguarded the crew and Orion systems as the spacecraft reentered Earth’s atmosphere. This test flight was the first time astronauts flew aboard Orion.

Orion reached a maximum velocity of 39 times the speed of sound and experienced external temperatures exceeding 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit at its peak, all while the four astronauts inside Orion stayed relatively cool with a cabin temperature in the mid-70 degree Fahrenheit range during their return to Earth from the Moon.

After NASA’s thorough analysis of Artemis I heat shield findings, informed by extensive arc jet material testing at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley, the agency modified Orion’s reentry trajectory for Artemis II by shortening the maximum downrange distance the spacecraft could fly between when it entered Earth’s atmosphere and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean. Analysis prior to the mission showed that limiting downrange distance would limit how long the spacecraft’s heat shield spent in the temperature range at which the Artemis I heat shield phenomenon occurred.

The spacecraft reentered with precision, entering within only 192 feet of its targeted entry interface, and successfully splashed down only 0.59 miles from the predicted landing site off the coast of San Diego. Initial inspections of the thermal protection system, including diver imagery of the spacecraft’s heat shield taken just after splashdown and further inspections on the recovery ship, found it performed as expected, with a significant reduction in the amount of cracks and char loss as compared to Artemis I.

Upon the spacecraft’s return to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida after the Moon mission, thermal protection system experts began additional examination of the heat shield, made of 186 unique blocks of an ablative material called Avcoat. The heat shield was then transported to NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, where work on sample extraction and internal x-ray scans began in August to provide further engineering insight into the system and behavior of the material.

A thorough post-flight assessment review found that Orion’s aerodynamic and aerothermal performance, including the heat shield and backshell thermal protection system, was in line with engineering predictions based on pre-flight analyses and ground testing. The shorter allowable down range during entry reduced the cracking and char loss experienced on the Artemis II heat shield relative to the Artemis I heat shield by a factor of ten, proving the effectiveness of the trajectory modification. Engineers found only nine spots of char loss of varying sizes on the Artemis II heat shield dish, compared to 103 during Artemis I.

The analysis also showed that Orion’s robust heat shield design showed consistency from Artemis I to Artemis II, evident by the performance of system features such as the seams between the heat shield Avcoat blocks and the Avcoat surrounding the heat shield compression pad separation bolts.

Post-flight inspection of Orion’s backshell, the protective cover on the sloped sides of the crew module made up of 1,300 ceramic tiles, showed expected performance across the crew module surface. Visual inspections indicated backshell features designed to seal and protect penetrations such as windows, vents, thrusters, and the side hatch also met expectations, with no signs of overheating observed.

The team also performed post-flight laser scans of the heat shield surface and is comparing this data to pre-flight measurements to determine material recession, which will then be compared to analysis predictions. Engineers are continuing with heat shield sample extraction at NASA Marshall and subsequent material test and assessment and thermal analysis, to support long-term heat shield development, manufacturing efforts, and data capture.

Orion’s performance and the team’s analysis on Artemis II reflect system robustness, capability to support crew, and critical insights gathered that will enhance the Artemis III mission and beyond. Following the extensive Artemis I heat shield investigation, upgrades were made to the heat shield design for Artemis III to achieve uniformity and consistent permeability of the Avcoat blocks. Technicians attached the heat shield for the Artemis III Orion crew module at NASA Kennedy in early July, and the Orion crew and service modules were joined at the end of July. The spacecraft has since been successfully powered up for the first time, enabling engineers to check all connection lines between the two modules are working as planned.

NASA continues to advance toward Artemis III as teams ready the Orion spacecraft for next year’s mission in low Earth orbit. NASA will launch the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and Orion spacecraft with NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) Luca Parmitano, to rendezvous with human lander test articles from Blue Origin and SpaceX to demonstrate critical systems and operations needed for future lunar landings, beginning with Artemis IV in 2028.

item.title: Life after the moon: Artemis II's Christina Koch steps down from active astronaut duty - Space
item.description:
Don't expect any of the Artemis II moon astronauts to fly again soon.

On Tuesday (Oct. 13), NASA announced that Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch will become the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1.

"With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments," NASA officials wrote in a statement on Tuesday.

Her three Artemis II crewmates had already shared their next moves, none of which put another spaceflight in play in the near future.

Mission commander Reid Wiseman and pilot Victor Glover, both of NASA, became "emeritus" astronauts last month, a role that seems to include planning, advising and mentoring duties but no flights into the final frontier. Glover will also work full-time at his alma mater, the California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly) in San Luis Obispo.

"I'm grateful they will continue sharing what they learned with our astronauts, flight controllers and engineers as we prepare for Artemis III in 2027 and the missions that follow," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said of Wiseman and Glover in a Sept. 9 statement.

The fourth Artemis II astronaut, mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of the Canadian Space Agency, announced a change of his own in July: He planned to become a reservist in the Royal Canadian Air Force, where he's also a colonel. That move became official last month as well.

Artemis II sent the four astronauts on a 10-day trip around the moon in an Orion capsule. It was the first crewed mission of NASA's Artemis program and the first human spaceflight beyond low Earth orbit (LEO) since Apollo 17 in 1972.

As Isaacman mentioned, the next mission in the program is Artemis III, a docking test in LEO scheduled to launch next year. The Artemis III crew, which was announced in June, consists of NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik (commander), Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio (mission specialists) andLuca Parmitano of the European Space Agency (pilot).

If all goes according to plan, Artemis IV will land astronauts near the moon's south pole in 2028. We don't yet know who will fly on that historic mission.

Koch will succeed current NASA Deputy Chief Engineer Katherine Van Hooser, who will retire on Oct. 21 after more than 35 years of work for the space agency.

"In her new role, Koch will help lead NASA's engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness, and engineering excellence across the agency's programs and projects," agency officials said in Tuesday's statement.

Koch is a natural choice for the job, given her education and experience. She holds bachelor's degrees in electrical engineering and physics and a master's in electrical engineering, and she began her NASA career as an electrical engineer at Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland.

NASA selected Koch as an astronaut candidate in 2013. She has two spaceflights under her belt: Artemis II and a 328-day-flight to the International Space Station that launched in March 2019. That's the longest space mission ever conducted by a woman, and it featured the first three all-female spacewalks, which Koch conducted with fellow NASA astronaut Jessica Meir.

"Christina has seen NASA engineering from both sides of the equation: developing complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space," Isaacman said in the Tuesday statement.

"After spending nearly a year living and working aboard the International Space Station and helping lead America back around the moon on Artemis II this year, she brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role," he added. "I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface, build the Moon Base, get underway on nuclear power in space, and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

item.title: Astronaut Christina Koch trades spacesuit for desk in new role at NASA - USA Today
item.description:
Astronaut Christina Koch trades spacesuit for desk in new role at NASA

The news comes about six months after Koch was part of the four-person Artemis II crew that rode a NASA spacecraft on a 10-day journey toward the moon.

  • NASA astronaut Christina Koch is taking on a new role as the agency's acting deputy chief engineer.
  • Koch was part of the historic Artemis II mission, becoming the first woman to fly near the moon.
  • Her desk job means she will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments.
  • All four astronauts from the Artemis II crew have now stepped away from active spaceflight roles.

NASA astronaut Christina Koch is taking a new role at the agency after making history as the first woman to fly near the moon during the Artemis II mission in April.

Thirteen years after being selected as an astronaut, Koch plans to trade her spacesuit for a desk, NASA announced.

The news comes about six months after Koch was part of the four-person Artemis II crew that rode a NASA spacecraft on a 10-day journey toward the moon. The mission marked a landmark moment in U.S. spaceflight, becoming not just the first crewed moon mission in half-a-century, but taking the astronauts farther from Earth than anyone had ever been.

With Koch's announcement, all four of those astronauts have now stepped away from spaceflight to eye new career opportunities.

Here's what to know about Koch, as well as what's next for the record-setting NASA astronaut.

Artemis II astronaut takes on new role at NASA

Effective Nov. 1, Koch will become NASA's acting deputy chief engineer, NASA announced in an Oct. 13 press release. Koch will replace Katherine Van Hooser, who served in the role for 35 years.

The role means Koch will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments, NASA added.

"She brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement. " I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface ... and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars.”

Who is Christina Koch? About record-setting astronaut

A native of Grand Rapids, Michigan, Koch grew up in Jacksonville, North Carolina. Before she was selected for the Artemis II mission, Koch, an engineer, has already had a prolific, record-setting astronaut career.

First selected in the 2013 astronaut class, Koch made history in 2019 when she conducted the first all-woman spacewalk at the International Space Station. On Oct. 28, 2019, Koch spent more than seven hours suited up and exposed to the vacuum of space with astronaut Jessica Meir, who recently returned from the outpost for the second time as part of the Crew-12 mission.

Koch spent almost all of 2019 in space during her first mission, setting a record for the longest spaceflight for any American woman at 328 days. Just three other NASA astronauts have been on longer single missions than she has.

Koch, 47, is also an avid amateur hobbyist, whose favorite activities include surfing, rock climbing and adventuring.

What was the Artemis II mission?

In April, Koch joined NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Victor Glover, as well as the Canadian Space Agency's Jeremy Hansen on the Artemis II mission.

The second mission under NASA's multibillion-dollar Artemis program, Artemis II marked the first time humans flew near the moon in more than 50 years and set the stage for a potential crewed landing as early as 2028.

The four astronauts rode in NASA's Orion spacecraft, which hitched a ride to space atop NASA's powerful 322-foot Space Launch System rocket during an April 1 launch from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. During the 10-day spaceflight, the Orion vehicle carried the astronauts around the moon and back to Earth without landing on the lunar surface.

Along the way, Wiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen surpassed a record set during the infamous Apollo 13 mission in 1970 – traveling a historic 252,756 miles from Earth. They also bore witness to sights of the moon's far side never before seen by human eyes while traveling as close as 4,067 miles above the surface during a lunar flyby.

Three of the astronauts also made individual history. Hansen became the first Canadian selected for a moon mission, while Koch became the first woman and Glover the first Black man.

All 4 Artemis II crew members have stepped away from spaceflight

While Koch technically remains in active service, her announcement still means all four astronauts who flew on the Artemis II mission have now stepped away from spaceflight.

In September, Wiseman, the mission's commander; Victor Glover, the mission's pilot, also announced their plans to transition to an emeritus role at the U.S. space agency. Instead of officially retiring, Glover and Wiseman intend to essentially serve as consultants to NASA while seeking other professional opportunities.

Glover, for instance, has already accepted a full-time administrative leadership position at his alma mater, California Polytechnic State University in San Luis Obispo.

In July, Hansen said that he would step back from a full-time astronaut role as well with the Canadian Space Agency.

Eric Lagatta is the Space Connect reporter for the USA TODAY Network. Reach him at elagatta@usatodayco.com

item.title: Artemis III Scientist Shares What to Expect From NASA’s Next Lunar Mission - WIRED
item.description:
For years, NASA hoped to bring humans back to the moon’s surface, and Artemis III was going to be the mission to accomplish this feat. That will no longer be the case.

Following the successful Artemis II flyby last April, the program’s schedule was revised. According to the most recent announcements, the next mission will have to wait until 2028, and while the new plans are admittedly less spectacular than a lunar landing, they’re hardly dispensable.

In 2027, NASA plans to test in Earth orbit whether the Orion capsule can safely rendezvous and operate with commercial lunar landing systems from SpaceX and Blue Origin before attempting those same maneuvers around the moon. WIRED en Español spoke with Barbara Cohen, a scientist on the Artemis III project, to better understand this upcoming mission—the conversation ranging from the role humans still play in the face of increasingly capable robots and sensors to what we can learn about the solar system’s violent past from traces preserved on the moon.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

JORGE GARAY: What should people expect from Artemis III, and why does this mission matter even if it won’t land astronauts on the moon?

BARBARA COHEN: Artemis III is an Earth-orbiting mission. That’s the one that’s coming up next. We will send the Orion capsule to Earth’s orbit with the people in it. Blue Origin and SpaceX are the companies that are making the lunar landers, so each one of those companies will make a test article. It won’t be the full lunar lander, but those companies will send their version of the test article into Earth’s orbit to meet up with Orion. This is to make sure that Orion can meet with the lunar landers, so that when they do go to lunar orbit, they can do that safely.

Where does science fit into the Artemis program, and what have you learned so far about how astronauts can contribute scientifically?

The Artemis missions, just to be clear, are not science missions. They’re exploration for a lot of different reasons. We do that for technology development. We do that for inspiration. And we try to get the science that we can from the opportunity. And so we still work really hard to identify unique science opportunities that exist because the mission exists.

One of the things on Artemis III we’re doing is like a dress rehearsal for bringing samples back from the moon. When we land on the moon and start to bring samples back, those samples change as soon as you take them out of their natural environment. We try to make sure that they change as little as possible, but they are going to change.

You have to bring them back and put them into curation so that scientists can study them. We want to understand every step along the way: What could be changing the samples, how the samples could be reacting, especially to the environment around them. So we’ll have our crew deploy these witness materials—pieces of aluminum foil, pieces of Teflon, maybe pieces of ceramic. They’re very clean surfaces, very small pieces, maybe the size of a quarter or a nickel. And the team will be opening those up and exposing them to the crew cabin throughout their flight. That’ll give us a feel for how the humans change the environment around them.

With the capabilities of probes and other robotic tools today, what is the purpose of sending human astronauts into space?

If you just want to take pictures, you do that with robotic assets. Robots can take pictures. They do that all the time. We have lots of pictures in the area. We also have, on the International Space Station, a way for us to ask, “Please take a picture of this. Please take a picture of that.” That’s not what we did with Artemis II, and that’s not what we’re trying to do with Artemis III or Artemis IV, V, VI. With the Artemis missions, we’re trying to use the humans to their best capability, and what the humans are really good at is seeing a wide scene, zooming in on details very naturally, and then trying to interpret what they’re seeing and take the next step.

We don’t know everything about the moon. To learn more, we need to literally go on the surface and figure out what’s there and where to go next. So some of this is trying to train—not just the crew onboard—but the flight directors and the science team and the engineers. We all need to work together to enable humans to do what they do best.

We also give the crew science prompts. We say, “What do you think is happening in this scene? There’s something like a storm or an algal bloom or a fire. What do you see? How do you see the scene changing? What do you think that means? What do you think is causing that change? What do you think is going to happen next? If you could do anything, what would you do next?” That helps us understand what they’re looking at, which is not just taking pictures. It’s making observations, making understanding, making inferences with their brains. That’s what humans are really good at. That’s what we’ll be asking them to do.

From a science point of view, we learned a lot about how crew really wants to use their powers of observation, and how we should participate in the observations and train them in the science that we want them to do. We also had the ability to include science directly in flight. On Artemis II, we had our science officer talk directly to crew. That was a new thing that we’ll be carrying forward to Artemis III and beyond.

When humans return to the lunar surface, what scientific questions would you most like Artemis to help answer?

I have a personal opinion. My personal scientific interest is how old craters on the moon are. If you look at the moon—with binoculars or a small telescope, or even in pictures—you see that it is covered in craters. In fact, we call it saturated, because every crater that forms does so on another crater. The whole surface is covered in craters. The Earth is not, but I promise you that for every crater that formed on the moon, there was a crater that formed on Earth.

The moon doesn’t get hit more than the Earth, but we have a lot of water. We have erosion on our continents. Our continents move around. They get subducted. We get new land that forms. All of those processes on the Earth erase craters. And so, if we want to know what was hitting the Earth in the past—and I promise you that things were hitting the Earth—we can’t find that evidence on the Earth anymore. We’ve erased it. So we have to go to the moon to figure that out.

There was a period in time when the solar system was forming—4.5 billion years ago, 4 billion years ago. Humans weren’t around. Life hadn’t arisen on Earth yet. We think that the solar system was very dynamic, and there were a lot of impacts happening, a lot of material being exchanged. So there were a lot of craters—big, big craters, basin-size craters, craters the size of continents. They really disrupted the moon, and they would have disrupted the Earth as well. Like I said, we don’t have any evidence of that because we don’t have any rocks from that time anymore. But it’s really worth knowing. Did we disrupt the Earth several times? How did life get going? How did we get nutrients? How did material move around the solar system? That evidence is preserved on the moon.

There is a big crater called the South Pole-Aitken Basin. It’s on the lunar far side, but it intersects the South Pole of the moon, where we expect humans to be going. It would be my personal desire that humans could collect pieces of that big crater, and we could understand when it formed and what it did to the moon and what was happening in the solar system at that time.

Artemis III won’t do that just yet. Lunar touchdown is currently expected as part of Artemis IV, which is expected to take off in early 2028. Before then, the upcoming third mission will have to demonstrate something far less spectacular, but crucial for the program’s future: That the spacecraft, procedures, and the people who will one day carry out these missions can work together safely.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

item.title: NASA Completes Artemis III Booster Stacking, Shares Status Update - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA Completes Artemis III Booster Stacking, Shares Status Update

Progress on NASA’s Artemis III’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket continues at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, where teams have completed the integration of the final solid rocket booster motor segments onto the mobile launcher for the “short stack” configuration that will be used during a tanking test. Teams also completed installation of all four RS-25 engines on the SLS core stage.

Teams now will install the systems tunnel that runs the length of the core stage and is used to route pyrotechnic cabling, a system of wiring that allows the single-use, quick disconnect for controlled movements during liftoff, on the massive stage. In the coming weeks, the stage will be integrated with the solid rocket boosters, completing the rocket’s “short stack” configuration.

NASA will roll the short stack SLS rocket from the spaceport’s Vehicle Assembly Building to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test in the coming months, where the Artemis launch team will practice procedures and timelines for loading propellant. While at the pad, the Artemis III crew, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano, also will conduct a launch day rehearsal and emergency exit walkdown. This will include suiting up in astronaut crew quarters, driving to the launch pad, ascending the mobile launcher, and then walking through the exit route they would take in the unlikely event of an emergency during launch countdown.

Additional hardware updates

At Launch Pad 39B, teams continue the refurbishment of the flame deflector, which saw minimal damage after the Artemis II launch. The bricks on the flame trench itself were not affected by the launch due to ground support improvements informed by lessons learned after Artemis I in 2022.

Teams are continuing to work through testing on the Orion spacecraft. Recently, engineers with ESA and Airbus inspected the solar array wings, which deliver power to the service module that provides propulsion, thermal control, and electrical power to the spacecraft, as well as air and water for the crew.

At NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, the forward and aft rings were welded on the Artemis III spacer, completing the primary structure. The spacer will serve to represent upper stage dimensions during the mission. The dimensional checks are underway.

Engineers also are converting two existing structural test articles, the Orion stage adapter and launch vehicle stage adapter, into flight-ready hardware. Exterior painting on the Orion stage adapter was recently completed at NASA Marshall, with cables and brackets to be installed soon. The launch vehicle stage adapter has undergone detailed inspection and preparation, with corrosion removal nearly complete, and nondestructive evaluation will begin this fall. Following that evaluation, technicians will apply conversion coating to the interior, prime and paint the exterior, and spray the cone-shaped adapter with thermal protection spray foam.

The spacer and both adapters remain on track to ship to Kennedy early next year.

Crew training continues

The Artemis III crew has continued a variety of training activities to prepare for their mission. Recently, they completed lessons on the flywheel exercise device, practicing hardware setup, anticipated exercises, and equipment disassembly. This compact device, about the size of an extra-large shoe box, uses pulleys and a torque limiter to mimic a rowing machine, allowing aerobic, resistive, and rowing exercises with straps attached to either a bar or harness.

Nutrition also is a key focus. At NASA’s Space Food Systems Laboratory in Houston, crew members sampled nearly 200 items on the menu to select their favorites for the mission, ensuring their health and performance are supported throughout.

The crew concluded helicopter underwater egress training, practicing escape from a submerged, upside-down mock helicopter cabin in a controlled pool environment to prepare for potential off-nominal water crash-landings.

Last week, members of the Artemis III crew traveled to San Diego to participate in recovery training with NASA and military partners, practicing water lifts by U.S. Navy helicopters.

They completed several suited training activities in the Orion Crew Survival System Suits this week, preparing for post-insertion, deorbit procedures, and emergency responses. These activities included communication system checks, suit operations, emergency equipment handling, contingency drills, and cabin configuration with stowage, ensuring the crew is ready for any scenario that may arise.

In September, the full Artemis III crew and backup astronauts visited Florida together for the first time since their crew announcement earlier this year. The astronauts visited their Orion spacecraft, saw the integrated solid rocket boosters on top of the mobile launcher, and viewed the core stage undergoing final processing ahead of integration. The crew also visited commercial partners SpaceX and Blue Origin to become more oriented with the lunar lander providers’ progress, marking one more milestone in preparation for the daring Artemis III mission.

item.title: NASA to Discuss Artemis Acceleration, Status of Upcoming Moon Missions - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA will provide an update on its plans to return American astronauts to the surface of the Moon by 2028 at 2 p.m. EDT, Friday, Oct. 23, at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Learn where to watch online:

Participants in the briefing include:

  • NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman
  • NASA Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya
  • Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager

The update will include details about NASA’s Artemis III mission that will send four astronauts to low Earth orbit next year to test critical systems needed for future lunar landings, and how plans to return American astronauts to the Moon by 2028 are progressing.

U.S. media interested in attending in person must apply online by 12 p.m., Friday, Oct. 16. To ask questions remotely, media must request the dial-in number from the Kennedy newsroom no later than one hour prior to the start of the update by emailing: ksc-newsroom@mail.nasa.gov. NASA’s media accreditation policy is online.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

item.title: NASA Starts Artemis III Engine Install; Boosters, Crew Training Advance - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
NASA Starts Artemis III Engine Install; Boosters, Crew Training Advance

Technicians at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began the installation of the four RS-25 engines in the core stage of the agency’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket that will launch the Artemis III crew next year.

The milestone on Aug. 24 marks the next phase of core stage integration following the mating of the engine section to the top four-fifths of the stage earlier this summer. Inside High Bay 2 at the spaceport’s Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB), teams will continue installing the remaining engines, as well as the propulsion and electrical systems throughout the stage.

Weighing in at approximately 7,700 pounds, each engine produces nearly 500,000 pounds of thrust. All four engines are located at the base of the SLS and are integrated inside the engine section. Built to withstand the extreme conditions during launch, this section protects the engines from severe temperatures. During ascent, the engines fire continuously for more than eight minutes, consuming propellant from the core stage’s two massive propellant tanks at a rate of approximately 1,500 gallons per second.

Each RS-25 engine carries a unique serial number that traces its detailed flight history. The four engines assigned to Artemis III, including E2054, E2057, E2048, and E2052, previously powered multiple shuttle missions. Engine 2048 helped power NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik’s previous mission on space shuttle Atlantis during the STS-129 mission. The engine also powered Space Shuttle Discovery on STS-95 in 1998, which was the mission that returned 77-year-old space pioneer U.S. Sen. John Glenn to orbit, making him the oldest person to fly in space at the time.

Technicians also continue to integrate the twin solid rocket booster motor segments atop the mobile launcher inside the VAB. Teams began stacking the segments in early July and are now more than halfway complete after streamlining processes and procedures learned from previous Artemis launches.

Progress on the Orion spacecraft continues after the recent integration of the crew and service modules. Technicians recently installed the umbilical connector, which bridges the electrical, data, and fluid systems between the two modules, and installed its electrical connectors and fluid lines. Teams powered on the spacecraft for the first time since joining the two components to ensure electrical connectivity through the umbilical mechanism and that the communications of the subsystems between the crew and service module work as planned.

Crew training underway

After being assigned to the Artemis III mission on June 9, NASA astronauts Bresnik, Andre Douglas, Frank Rubio, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano began an intensive training flow that covers Orion systems and operations, science objectives, leadership and team‑building exercises, as well as joint training with commercial human landing system providers.

The crew’s training is organized around major phases of the mission, including ascent, orbit and rendezvous operations, entry, and both pre‑ and post‑landing readiness.

Crew members are working in the Orion mockup at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, practicing daily spacecraft operations, such as mealtime routines, using equipment like the food warmer and potable water dispenser. They also are refining their camera skills to capture and share imagery from their mission in low Earth orbit.

The crew recently completed an introductory water survival class focused on hardware used during off‑nominal landings, along with a post‑landing emergency exiting course that introduced splashdown procedures and initial post‑landing conditions.

This week in NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Lab, they donned their spacesuits and practiced exiting Orion in an upright configuration. The practice allowed the crew to demonstrate the proper use of their Orion Crew Survival System suits, survival hardware, life raft, and more.

The Artemis III crew also began integrated simulations with the flight control team, including the first simulation with the four crew members together. In these sessions, crew members and controllers rehearse mission timelines and respond to a variety of situations they could face in space, strengthening coordination, decision‑making, and procedures.

item.title: Artemis II Crew Moon Photo Annotations - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
A visualization of a dark Moon eclipsing the Sun is marked with handwritten notes in this April 6, 2026, screenshot from an Artemis II crew member’s tablet.

NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (in blue) and Victor “Ike” Glover (in green) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) Jeremy Hansen (in red) observed impact flashes and their locations, which are noted on the image. Overall, the astronauts reported seeing five extremely faint “pinprick” bursts of light from their view aboard Orion, which was 46,000 miles away from the Moon at the time. These flashes are sparked by rocky fragments hitting the Moon.

From April 1 through April 10, 2026, NASA’s Artemis II crew traveled to the Moon and back and along the way, captured stunning imagery and scientific observations of our nearest neighbor. Now, the full lunar science dataset from their journey is available to the global science community, and to the public, for further study. Read about the report, listen to crew audio observations, and explore more.

item.description:
NASA Releases Artemis II Lunar Science Data, Images

NASA’s Artemis II crew traveled around the Moon and back and, along the way, captured stunning imagery and scientific observations of our nearest neighbor. NASA is making the full lunar science dataset from their journey available Wednesday to the global science community and the public for further study.

More than 800 gigabytes of Artemis II lunar science data – some previously unreleased – have been uploaded to NASA’s Planetary Data System, the public archive for NASA’s planetary missions. This data release includes more than 11,000 full-resolution images and video of the Moon from the crew’s handheld cameras and the Orion spacecraft’s cameras, 8.5 hours of audio recordings of the crew’s scientific observations of the lunar surface, and crew-annotated images.

When combined, the images, audio files, and crew notes from the expedition provide a powerful lunar science dataset ripe for exploration and analysis. This is the first planetary science dataset captured primarily by humans in more than half a century and humanity’s influence on it is clear. Through training in classrooms, simulations, and field environments, NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen developed expertise in lunar geography, geology, and observational best practices. Their quick decisions about observation targets and which images to capture, along with their perceptions of color and dynamic changes, and discussions about the science of the lunar surface and its surroundings complement decades of data from Apollo astronauts and robotic explorers and deepen our understanding of the Moon as NASA prepares for long-term exploration of the lunar surface.

Along with this data, NASA has released the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide. Together, these three publications provide an overview of the Artemis II lunar mission data and activities, and a technical summary of how the science plan was developed and implemented. This information is already helping inform NASA’s exploration plans for Artemis III and beyond.

item.title: Core rocket for upcoming Artemis III mission arrives at Kennedy Space Center - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
item.description:
Core rocket for upcoming Artemis III mission arrives at Kennedy Space Center

NASA engineers will complete the assembly of the massive rocket.

The Artemis II astronauts may have just returned from a successful mission to the moon, but NASA engineers are already preparing for the upcoming Artemis III launch.

The largest section of the rocket for the Artemis III mission arrived at the Kennedy Space Center in Merritt Island, Florida, on Monday, according to NASA.

The 212-foot-long Space Launch System (SLS) core stage was manufactured at NASA’s Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans before traveling 900 miles aboard a barge to the space center, where the complete assembly will take place.

The core stage contains the liquid hydrogen tank, liquid oxygen tank, intertank and forward skirt, according to NASA.

On Tuesday, the top four-fifths of the core stage were transported to NASA's Vehicle Assembly, where it will be integrated with the boat-tail and engine section to complete the full stage assembly.

NASA hosted a live stream of the unloading and transportation of the core stage to the Vehicle Assembly Building.

The historic 10-day Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1 and splashed down on April 10, took the four-person crew on a 694,481-mile journey around the moon.

The lunar fly-by allowed the astronauts to observe unprecedented views of the moon's Orientale basin with the human eye for the first time.

The next mission, Artemis III, will test rendezvous and docking capabilities between the Orion spacecraft and commercial spacecraft that will be used to land astronauts on the moon.

The demonstration mission in low Earth orbit will test one or both commercial landers from SpaceX and Blue Origin, respectively.

The Artemis III crew is expected to launch Orion on the SLS rocket from the Kennedy Space Center in late 2027, according to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

Humanity will return to the moon's surface during the Artemis IV mission, expected to launch in 2028, according to NASA.

The current plan for Artemis IV calls for the astronauts to travel to lunar orbit, where crew members will descend to the surface near the South Pole of the moon to conduct tests. They will then rejoin the rest of the crew in lunar orbit and journey back to Earth.

Artemis IV will mark the first lunar landing with humans since Apollo 17 in 1972.

item.title: NASA's Artemis III is about three months behind schedule, Isaacman says - Mashable
item.description:
NASA's Artemis III mission is about three months behind schedule, administrator Jared Isaacman says, putting pressure on the agency's plan to launch two moon-landing missions in 2028.

In a wide-ranging email to employees on Sunday, Isaacman said Artemis III could launch in the summer of 2027, preserving two opportunities for lunar landings the following year. But that's the "best-case scenario."

NASA doesn't plan to put astronauts on the moon during Artemis III. The agency redesigned the mission earlier this year as a crewed flight in Earth orbit, wherein astronauts would rehearse docking the Orion spacecraft with lunar landers built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. The test is intended to practice those crucial space maneuvers close to home and reduce risk before the first Artemis moon landing.

You May Also Like

The 90-day delay represents a meaningful setback for an agency that has spent this year trying to accelerate the Artemis campaign, leveraging the momentum of the successful Artemis II flight around the moon. It also comes as Isaacman frames the agency's return to the surface as a broader competition with China. That makes NASA's current pace more consequential than a typical schedule slip.

"Perpetuating the status quo is not an achievable strategy in this race," Isaacman said. "There is simply too much on the line."

The disclosure of the schedule tension reveals how much ground NASA needs to make up if it wants Artemis IV and V, the first two landing missions of the program, to launch in 2028. If Artemis III continues to lag, NASA might be looking at just one shot to put boots on the moon in late 2028, Isaacman said in the email, published online Monday by NASA Watch, former NASA employee Keith Cowing's blog. NASA has since confirmed the email's authenticity to Mashable.

and tech news delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for

Mashable's Light Speed newsletter

or

get Mashable push alerts

today.

NASA announced an overhaul to the Artemis architecture in February, wedging this 2027 mission in between Artemis II's lunar flyby and the first crewed landing. Since then, the agency has announced the Artemis III astronauts: Commander Randy Bresnik, Andre Douglas, Frank Rubio, and European pilot Luca Parmitano. 

That major redesign has meant sidelining a complicated project to build an orbiting lunar space station, called Gateway, that would have served as both a lab and pit stop for lunar missions. NASA has since pivoted to building a moon base on the surface instead. 

The base is expected to sit at the lunar south pole, a region about the size of Virginia. The area is coveted for its deep, shadowed craters that may hold ancient ice and other frozen material. If NASA can learn to harness those resources for water and fuel, astronauts could avoid needing constant resupplies from Earth and become more self-sufficient.

"Had we stayed the course with Gateway, China was positioned to advance landers equipped with rovers and hopper drones, drone capabilities we ourselves did not have in development until recently, and potentially deny access to the most desirable locations on the surface," Isaacman said.

But the new schedule has exposed friction across the program. NASA is working directly with suppliers and subcontractors to get delayed components, including valves and parts used to steer the rocket, back on track, Isaacman said. It's even making some hardware itself to accelerate production.

In Sunday's message, the administrator reiterated that the moon campaign isn't about merely getting there and planting another U.S. flag in the moondust.

"We are making sure that when America returns to the Moon, we can actually stay," he said.

item.title: Next Artemis mission on track for 2027, but anything can happen, astronaut says - Reuters
item.description:
Item 1 of 3 Astronauts Randy Bresnik, Luca Parmitano, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas are unveiled as the NASA Artemis III mission crew at an event at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, U.S., June 9, 2026. REUTERS/Antranik Tavitian/File Photo

[1/3]Astronauts Randy Bresnik, Luca Parmitano, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas are unveiled as the NASA Artemis III mission crew at an event at NASA Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, U.S., June 9,... Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tabRead more

Summary

Companies

NASA's third Artemis mission a docking rehearsal in Earth's orbit

Moon landers from SpaceX, Blue Origin face delays

Meetings planned over the next few months to determine readiness of the landers

WASHINGTON, Oct 5 (Reuters) - The next mission under NASA's Artemis moon program could still launch ​next summer as planned, but "anything can happen" given the remaining development work for the two lunar landers needed for ‌the mission, one of the Artemis III astronauts told Reuters.

NASA's third Artemis mission will be the first to involve the program's moon landers — SpaceX's (SPCX.O), opens new tab Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon.

Unlike Artemis II, the spacecraft will stay in Earth's orbit to perform crewed docking demonstrations with Orion, a capsule whose job is to transfer the ​astronaut crew to the landers after getting them into space.

"The biggest thing is having faith in the team to pull ​together, with the same rationale that anything can happen," Artemis III mission specialist Andre Douglas said in ⁠an interview on Monday, when asked if Artemis III is still on track for launch next year.

Douglas, 40, fellow NASA astronauts Randy ​Bresnik and Frank Rubio, as well as Italian astronaut Luca Parmitano, were tapped this year as the crew for Artemis III, seen as a ​key rehearsal before NASA attempts to put astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028 in Artemis IV.

Both companies' lunar landers have had scheduledelays while facing an unchecked list of complex development tasks, such as demonstrating the ability to store and delicately transfer super-cooled propellants in space and dock with another object in orbit.

"Those ​are the major ones," Douglas said of the milestones the contractors need to achieve before the mission.

While some industry sources doubt the landers ​will be ready in time for a 2027 mission, NASA has been optimistic, with administrator Jared Isaacman citing good progress for "the parts that are in NASA's ‌greatest control," ⁠referring to the NASA-owned Orion and its Space Launch System rocket.

Starship and Blue Moon have received billions of dollars in NASA funding while their development remains privately managed, a commercial-focused contracting model that has given NASA relatively little control over the manner and speed with which the companies build their landers.

"We just have to keep putting our heads down, leaning forward, and trying to meet the ideal timeline, which ​would be June of next ​year," said Douglas, who works ⁠with both SpaceX and Blue Origin on their lander development.

He added that he and other NASA officials plan to meet with SpaceX and Blue Origin over the next few months to determine their spacecraft's ​readiness.

The Artemis III mission had originally been planned as the program's first moon landing until February, when ​Isaacman imposed sweeping ⁠program changes that turned Artemis III into an extra practice mission. The agency is pressed to return to the moon quickly as it races China, which is targeting 2030 for its own first moon landing.

Artemis III will be the first trip to space for Douglas, who spent years ⁠shadowing the Artemis ​II crew as a backup. A systems engineering scholar and naval architect, Douglas has ​a background in the US Coast Guard that taught him how to be adaptable to rapid change, he said.

"I learned in the military that the plan only lasts ​for 10 minutes," he said. "You have expectations, but then you're also ready in the background for change."

Reporting by Joey Roulette Editing by Bill Berkrot

Joey Roulette is a space reporter for Reuters covering the business and politics of the global space industry, often focusing on space power competition and how commercial interests intersect with international relations. He was part of a team that won the 2024 Pulitzer Prize in national reporting for Reuters' coverage of Elon Musk's business empire. On the space beat for roughly a decade, Joey previously worked for the New York Times, the Verge, and various publications in Florida.

The four leaders of US President Donald Trump's ​AI task force are slated to meet on Thursday, task ‌force vice chair Scott Kupor told Reuters, adding that he expects the full committee to convene next week as pressure builds on Washington to take action on AI.

item.title: NASA Marches Toward Artemis III Mission in 2027, Names Crew Members - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
Taking another step toward one of the most complex human spaceflight missions in recent history, NASA on Tuesday provided new Artemis III details and announced the four prime crew members and a backup for the test flight. The mission will undertake a series of challenging tests in Earth orbit in 2027, essential for Artemis IV, the first planned crewed mission to the lunar South Pole in 2028.

During Artemis III, the agency’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket will launch the Orion spacecraft and its crew from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida to low Earth orbit. After Orion systems checkouts, the spacecraft will, for the first time, demonstrate rendezvous and docking capabilities with test versions from one, or both, American commercial human landing systems in development by Blue Origin and SpaceX. This highly choreographed mission includes a dramatic multi-launch campaign of the world’s most powerful rockets, testing integrated hardware between Orion and the landers, including system interfaces, software, propulsion, and communications.

Crew assignments are as follows:

  • NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, commander
  • ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano, pilot
  • NASA astronaut Andre Douglas, mission specialist
  • NASA astronaut Frank Rubio, mission specialist

As part of Tuesday’s event, NASA astronaut Bob Hines was named as a backup crew member. The crew will begin training immediately on Orion spacecraft systems, as well as assist in the development and operations of the test versions of Blue Origin and SpaceX landers.

“Today we take another bold step in humanity’s return to the Moon, building on the extraordinary foundation laid by the Artemis II astronauts,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Their achievements reignited global excitement for exploration, and now they pass the torch to the Artemis III team, Randy, Luca, Frank, and Andre. Artemis III will demonstrate the power of American innovation and international partnership as we test complex rendezvous and docking operations and advance the technologies that will one day carry us deeper into the solar system. This mission will require the most awe-inspiring coordination of heavy-lift rocket launches in history, drawing on the talent and capability of teams across government and the spaceflight community. The Artemis III astronauts, alongside ESA and our international partners, and the tens of thousands of the best and brightest across the agency and industry, are ushering in a new Golden Age of exploration carrying forward the hopes and dreams of the next generation just as the Apollo astronauts did for so many of us.”

This also is the first time an ESA astronaut has been assigned an Artemis mission.

“Artemis III will push the boundaries of spacecraft operations in orbit. Luca’s assignment as pilot reflects the depth of European expertise in human spaceflight and draws on his extensive operational experience in high-pressure situations,” said Josef Aschbacher, ESA’s director general. “At the same time, ESA’s European Service Module will once again provide the critical capabilities that power Orion, demonstrating Europe’s enduring role at the very heart of the Artemis program. The news out of Houston today is a powerful recognition of ESA’s role in enabling humanity’s return to the Moon – and a key advancement in our partnership with NASA. Europeans can take pride in being part of this exciting journey.”

Mission progress

NASA and its partners are making progress preparing for the test flight.

Engineers will connect the Orion crew module and service module this summer and integrate the spacecraft’s docking system, which will fly for the first time. Heat shield testing continues with individual blocks having undergone ultra-sonic inspections and installation onto the heat shield structure.

Rocket processing also is well underway. Technicians for SLS are integrating the engine section to the rest of the core stage ahead of installing the four RS-25 engines this summer. With all solid rocket booster segments now at NASA Kennedy and mobile launcher refurbishments on track, rocket stacking also is scheduled to begin this summer. NASA continues design and fabrication of a spacer that will replace the upper stage on Artemis III.

Blue Origin is developing a crewed lunar version of the company’s Blue Moon lander, while SpaceX is developing a crewed lunar lander version of the company’s Starship, with both companies building test articles for Artemis III. NASA is supporting both lander providers hands-on throughout design, development, testing, and evaluation, including sharing agency expertise and capabilities gained from previous missions.

In addition to status updates from NASA and both commercial partners, the agency discussed details during the event about the planned operations for Artemis III, which will support an increased mission cadence, ramp up production, and drive supply chain improvements for the Artemis program.

The Artemis III mission builds on the successful Artemis II flight completed in April and will help the agency prepare to send the first astronauts, Americans, to Mars.

Artemis III includes launching the world’s most powerful rockets in short order. Blue Origin’s lander pathfinder, which is able to stay in orbit for multiple weeks, will launch first and await the crew. NASA will send the astronauts aboard Orion by SLS to orbit Earth, before rendezvousing in space with the company’s lander test article and spending about two days docked together for tests and technology demonstrations, including entering the lander.

After completing docked operations with Blue Origin, Orion will detach and await Starship. SpaceX’s Starship pathfinder will launch and meet up with Orion to spend about a day connected for checkouts and testing. After that, Orion and its crew will undock and return home, splashing safely down in the Pacific Ocean where a team from the U.S. Navy and NASA will recover the astronauts.

In total, the crew is expected to remain in space for about two weeks, with exact mission length to be determined in real-time based on launch, rendezvous, and docked operations.

Learn more about Artemis III crew members

This will be the third mission to space for Bresnik, having launched aboard space shuttle Atlantis on the STS-129 mission to the International Space Station in 2009. He later flew on the Soyuz MS-05 spacecraft from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan to the space station, serving as a flight engineer for the station’s Expedition 52 and commander of Expedition 53. A California native, he graduated from The Citadel with a degree in mathematics and was selected by NASA in the 2004 astronaut candidate class. A retired U.S. Marine colonel, he has logged more than 7,000 hours in 95 types of aircraft and is a fellow in the Society of Experimental Test Pilots. Since 2018, he has served as assistant to the chief of the Astronaut Office for exploration, overseeing the development and testing of the spacecraft and systems that will operate during Artemis missions.

Artemis III also will be the third spaceflight for Parmitano. Selected by ESA as an astronaut in 2009, he first served as a flight engineer on the Italian Space Agency’s (ASI) first long-duration mission to the space station, launching on a Soyuz from Baikonur in 2013. He returned to the orbital laboratory in 2019 aboard Soyuz MS-13 for his second mission, during which he served as commander of Expedition 61, becoming the third European, and the first Italian, to command the station. Parmitano earned a bachelor’s degree in political sciences from the University of Naples Federico II and a master’s degree in experimental flight test engineering from the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace in Toulouse, France. A graduate of the Italian Air Force Academy, he became a test pilot in 2007 and was promoted to colonel in 2019. He has logged more than 2,000 flight hours across 40 types of aircraft.

Rubio is making his second trip to space. He launched aboard the Soyuz MS-22 spacecraft from Baikonur to the space station on Sept. 21, 2022, and returned on Sept. 27, 2023, breaking the record for the longest single-duration spaceflight by an American astronaut with 371 days in orbit. Rubio was selected by NASA in the 2017 astronaut candidate class. A Florida native, he graduated from the U.S. Military Academy in 1998, earned a doctor of medicine from the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences in 2010, and has served for more than 28 years in the U.S. Army as an aviator, a physician, and an astronaut.

The mission is Douglas’ first spaceflight. Selected by NASA in the 2021 astronaut candidate class, he previously served as a backup and closeout crew member for the agency’s Artemis II mission. A Virginia native, Douglas earned a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from the U.S. Coast Guard Academy and four postgraduate degrees from various institutions, including a doctorate in systems engineering from George Washington University. During his time in the Coast Guard, he conducted search and rescue, maritime salvage, and drug interdiction operations. Additionally, his time at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory involved designing and testing multidomain autonomous vehicles, space exploration systems, and numerous undersea warfare platforms.

Serving as a backup crew member, Hines will train alongside Bresnik, Parmitano, Rubio, and Douglas. Should a primary crew member be unable to participate in the mission, he would join the Artemis III crew. Hines previously served as pilot of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-4 mission to the International Space Station. Selected by NASA in the 2017 astronaut candidate class, he served as a research pilot at the agency’s Johnson Space Center prior to his selection. He is a colonel in the U.S. Air Force with more than 27 years of service as an instructor pilot, fighter pilot, and test pilot.

As part of the Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions to explore more of the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface, and to build on our foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars.

Learn more about NASA’s Artemis program:

item.title: NASA Just Made Nearly 1 TB of Artemis II Data Available to the Public - WIRED
item.description:
NASA has just released about 800 gigabytes of scientific data generated by the Artemis II mission. The archive documenting the astronauts’ return to the far side of the moon includes 11,000 full-resolution images and videos, 8.5 hours of spoken observations, notes taken by the astronauts, transcripts, and photographs from the cameras aboard the Orion capsule.

The space agency describes this effort as the first set of planetary science data obtained outside Earth and—for the most part—directly by humans in more than half a century. The closest comparable precedent dates back to the Apollo era and its missions to the lunar surface.

In addition to the public database, NASA released three reports summarizing what was learned during the first crewed spacecraft mission to approach the moon in five decades. These are the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report, the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report, and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide.

Anyone can access the near terabyte of data, though the release is primarily intended for the scientific community. While the astronauts capture and collect the data during the mission, it’s the researchers on Earth who will be able to analyze it and produce new findings about the moon. The information may be particularly useful for planetary geologists, flight engineers, heliophysicists, experts in telecommunications and remote sensing, as well as specialists in meteoroid impacts.

For space and astronomy enthusiasts, some of the most accessible materials include mission transcripts and lunar photographs annotated by the astronauts themselves. NASA has centralized access through its Planetary Data System, the public repository where it stores data from its planetary missions. In the section dedicated to the moon, users can access Artemis II and browse the various available collections, documents, and files.

For a less technical exploration, the agency has also set up an Artemis II science page where you can download the three reports, view a selection of photographs, and access the mission’s audio library. Anyone wishing to work directly with the raw data can visit the Planetary Data System, where the scientific files and their metadata are available for individual download and analysis.

Initial analyses of some of the Artemis II data have already yielded several concrete results. The most clear-cut finding is the detection of five small meteoroid impacts on the lunar surface during the 54-minute eclipse observed by the Orion crew. Recording these flashes will improve estimates of how often fragments just a few centimeters in size strike the moon—a key factor in calculating the risks future bases, vehicles, and astronauts will face.

The observations also documented differences in color, brightness, and texture among various lunar regions, which scientists can compare with composition maps previously obtained from orbit. In addition, photographs taken near the terminator—the boundary between lunar day and night—show in great detail how the terrain and visibility change when the sun is very low on the horizon. These conditions will be common near the south pole, where NASA plans to conduct the next Artemis missions. These data can therefore help the astronauts anticipate challenges related to navigation, lighting, and terrain recognition.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

item.title: Historic Engines Take Their Place on Artemis III - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
On Aug. 24, technicians at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began installing the four RS‑25 engines in the core stage of the agency’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket that will carry the Artemis III crew into low Earth orbit in 2027.

Each RS‑25 engine has a unique serial number that records its detailed flight history. The four engines assigned to Artemis III — E2054, E2057, E2048, and E2052 — previously powered multiple space shuttle missions. Engine 2048 helped launch NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik’s earlier mission aboard space shuttle Atlantis during STS‑129. It also flew on Space Shuttle Discovery during STS‑95 in 1998, the mission that returned 77-year‑old space pioneer U.S. Sen. John Glenn to orbit, making him the oldest person to fly in space at that time.

item.title: How NASA’s Artemis III Lander Test Will Pave Way for Moon Landings - NASA (.gov)
item.description:
Before Artemis astronauts land on the Moon’s surface in 2028, NASA will conduct the Artemis III demonstration mission in 2027, allowing teams on Earth and in orbit to practice rendezvous and docking operations between commercial human landing systems and the Orion spacecraft. Data from that mission, along with future uncrewed demonstration missions at the Moon, will support astronaut safety and mission success for crewed lunar landings.

NASA is working with two American companies to develop the human landing systems that will safely transport astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface and back for future Artemis missions. For Artemis III, both SpaceX and Blue Origin will fly test versions, or test articles, of the crewed landers that will be used for future Moon landings. The lander test articles will launch by commercial rockets, while the Artemis III crew will launch to low Earth orbit in Orion atop the agency’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket.

Stage setting for crewed flights

NASA and the human landing system providers have been working closely together to plan and determine capabilities for the Artemis III mission. With missions fast approaching, both SpaceX and Blue Origin are optimizing hardware availability and capability. SpaceX plans to use the company’s latest version of Starship and basis of the future Starship HLS, called Version 3, while Blue Origin will test their planned HLS crew cabin, allowing each company to apply lessons learned prior to uncrewed and crewed missions on the Moon.

“Each human landing system provider has taken a different approach to the Artemis III mission,” said Steve Creech, program manager, Human Landing System Program, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. “Ultimately, SpaceX and Blue Origin have put forward a list of aggressive objectives and goals intended to complement upcoming uncrewed demonstration missions at the Moon so that we can gain both understanding and confidence in the spacecraft and launch vehicles prior to a crewed landing. The lander prototype designs will inform future development efforts and will continue to mature over the next year.”

For the Artemis III mission, the Blue Moon test lander will be based on Blue Origin’s current architecture for its Mark 2 crew lander, incorporating all the major avionics and flight software and control systems to ensure flight operations from this demonstration mission can directly translate to crewed lunar flights. Up to two crew members, donning orange Orion crew survival system suits, will open the hatch to enter the Blue Origin test lander. The production hardware must incorporate many of the same systems and subsystems, including an Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS), a crew cabin, and avionics.

The Blue Origin lander also will fly with an instrumented lunar surface spacesuit mass simulator. Like the suited “Moonikin” manikin that flew aboard Orion during the uncrewed Artemis I test flight, the low-fidelity spacesuit mass simulator will provide real-time feedback about the environment within the Blue Moon crew cabin.

SpaceX’s Starship lander test article will use a Starship Version 3, currently in production and testing, with an added docking system installed on the nose of the 171-foot (52-m) spacecraft, enabling NASA and SpaceX to evaluate how the entire integrated stack of Orion and the Starship test lander interact. NASA and SpaceX are identifying controllability and communications tests for the Artemis III mission. Astronauts will not enter the Starship test lander during Artemis III.

Launch cadence

NASA, SpaceX, and Blue Origin will launch three of the world’s most powerful rockets within a short timeframe of one another, exercising ground processing, launch crews, and facilities as well as control centers, networking, and data exchange at key sites across the country during two separate, back-to-back rendezvous and docking maneuvers between Orion and the lander test articles, before a safe splashdown of the Artemis III crew in Orion.

“Artemis III will be a highly choreographed dance with a demanding launch sequence across multiple launch pads and equally demanding mission operations for our ground and flight crews, making it one of the most complex and ambitious missions NASA has ever undertaken,” said Jeremy Parsons, Artemis program manager. “The demonstration mission will set the stage before our next giant leap. NASA’s expertise in systems engineering and integration, as well as launch and mission operations in low Earth orbit, will bring the mission together.”

For future crewed missions to the Moon, NASA and one of the commercial lander partners will execute a “dual launch campaign,” prepositioning the lander in orbit to await a crewed Orion, launched on SLS. Launching the three rockets in succession of one another for Artemis III offers a unique opportunity to practice launch processing and operations.

Blue Origin’s lander test article is planned to launch first and will be able to loiter in space for up to 30 days, allowing for checkouts in orbit prior to the launch of SLS and Orion from Launch Complex 39B at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The Blue Origin test article will launch at a set trajectory to meet a designated “parking” orbit for these systems checks.

Jeremy Parsons

Artemis program manager

Following the completion of Blue Origin’s rendezvous and docking operations testing and the Artemis III crewed launch on SLS, SpaceX will launch its Starship lander test article to rendezvous with Orion and its crew for its phase of on-orbit testing.

Throughout the Artemis III mission, Orion will fly in a circular orbit. All three rockets will have more launch opportunities than are available for a lunar mission and will be able to reach the designated mission altitude in a single launch.

Docking operations

During docking and undocking operations, Orion and the Artemis III crew will use the lander test articles as the targets, while Orion will operate as the chaser spacecraft. This is the same configuration planned for future crew landing mission to the Moon.

NASA will ensure both test landers are mission ready and crew safe prior to Artemis III. These verifications will be based on functional and performance requirements for the test lander designs and hazard controls for hardware and software, ensuring the Artemis III astronauts inside Orion are safe throughout both docking phases of the mission.

SpaceX and Blue Origin have already tested their docking capabilities for their respective landers on the ground. SpaceX’s docking capability was qualified in 2023; Blue Origin conducted development ground testing on its pressurized docking system earlier this year.

A key difference between the docking capabilities of both lander test articles will be the location of docking. Orion will dock along the side of the Blue Moon test lander, adjacent to the crew cabin. Later, Orion will dock nose-to-nose with the giant SpaceX test lander.

Software testing between spacecrafts will help demonstrate that the commercial human landing system prototypes and Orion can meet at a precise time and location in space. When Orion docks with the Blue Moon test lander, the Orion spacecraft’s software will control the docked spacecraft. Meanwhile, the SpaceX test article will control the docked spacecraft for the second portion of the mission. During the docking phases, teams with NASA and the commercial partners will be able to test hardware and software interoperability, as well as dynamics of how the integrated lander-Orion spacecraft moves in space.

Through the Artemis program, NASA will send astronauts to explore the Moon for scientific discovery, economic benefits, and to build the foundation for the first crewed missions to Mars – for the benefit of all.
